subtype: Restless boredom on a long afternoon [Actor]
passage: The summer holidays were in their third week, and the afternoon in the Pune flat was hot and endless. Vinita lay upside down on the sofa, feet on the wall. "I'm bo-o-ored." Mummy, working at the dining table, just said, "Mm." No suggestions. No phone. Vinita sighed at the ceiling fan. She counted its turns, lost count, sighed again. She rolled onto the floor. Under the sofa were a lost marble, a bottle cap and a comb. She lined them up. The marble was a king, the bottle cap a boat, the comb a bridge. By four o'clock, her brother Tejas was lying beside her, building a second kingdom out of pens, and they were at war.

qa.q: What did Vinita find under the sofa?
qa.a: A lost marble, a bottle cap and a comb.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling while counting the fan's turns?
qa.a: Vinita felt restless and bored, with nothing to do and nobody filling the time.

qa.q: Mummy chose to say only "Mm." Why did that choice help?
qa.a: By not rushing in with suggestions or a phone, Mummy left space for the boredom to turn into Vinita's own game.

qa.q: How might Tejas see Vinita's game on joining in?
qa.a: Tejas probably found it more fun than anything else in the flat that afternoon and was happy to build a rival kingdom.

grounding: A bored child on a holiday afternoon invents a game from things under the sofa when no adult fills the time.

subtype: Restless boredom on a long afternoon [Actor]
passage:
"Thakuma, I'm bored."
"Hmm." Kalyani Thakuma turned a page of her newspaper.
"I'm SO bored."
"Boredom is a good guest," she said. "Let it sit a while."
"That makes no sense." Arnab flopped onto the cool floor. "Can I have your phone?"
"No."
"Can we go out?"
"In this heat? No."
Arnab groaned for a long time. Then silence. Ten minutes later Thakuma looked up. Arnab had pulled the mosquito net off the bed and tied it between two chairs.
"What's this?"
"It's a spider's web. I'm the spider. You're a fly who got stuck. Say 'help.'"
"Help," said Thakuma, very seriously.
"Too late," said Arnab, and pounced.

qa.q: What did Arnab tie between two chairs?
qa.a: The mosquito net.

qa.q: What did Arnab want when asking for the phone and to go out?
qa.a: Arnab wanted something to fill the boredom quickly, because sitting with nothing felt unbearable.

qa.q: What choice did Thakuma make, and what came of it?
qa.a: Thakuma chose not to fill the time and let the boredom sit a while; after ten minutes Arnab invented a spider game.

qa.q: How might Thakuma feel playing the stuck fly?
qa.a: Thakuma seems amused and pleased, joining the game with a serious face and enjoying Arnab's imagination. 😊

grounding: A grandmother lets a bored child stay bored, and the child invents a spider-web game from a mosquito net.

subtype: Restless boredom on a long afternoon [Actor]
passage: I'm Vishal, and last Diwali holiday I thought I would die of boredom. No school, no cricket because everyone had gone to their villages, and the TV was broken. My sister Usha was reading. I walked round the house eleven times. I lay on the balcony and stared at the pigeons. Nobody gave me anything to do; Papa just said, 'Find something.' Then I noticed the pigeons always landed on the same wire in the same order. I started giving them names and writing down who came first. By evening I had a notebook called Pigeon League Table, and Usha wanted to join. We still keep it going on weekends.

qa.q: How many times did Vishal walk round the house?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: How did Vishal feel about the holiday before noticing the pigeons?
qa.a: Vishal felt terribly bored and restless, as if the empty days would never end.

qa.q: Papa only said "Find something." Why was that a helpful choice?
qa.a: Papa didn't fill the time for Vishal, so the long empty stretch pushed Vishal to notice the pigeons and invent the league table.

qa.q: How might Usha see the Pigeon League Table?
qa.a: Usha seemed curious and wanted to join, so it probably looked like a fun new game rather than a cure for boredom.

grounding: A child bored through a holiday notices pigeons on a wire and invents a league table when nobody fills the time.

subtype: Restless boredom on a long afternoon [Actor]
passage:
Childminder's note, Maria D'Costa, holiday afternoons, Wednesday.
Simran (9) arrived after lunch and announced, "I'm bored," four times in the first twenty minutes. She lay on the floor, then on the sofa, then under the table. I didn't offer the tablet or a craft; I told her she could help me fold clothes or find her own thing. She groaned.
At about quarter to three, she went quiet. I found her at the dining table with scrap paper, a stapler and my old newspaper. She had started "The Colony Times": a report on the new stray kitten, an interview with the watchman (she went down and asked him three questions), and a weather forecast: "Hot. Still hot."
When her mother came, Simran made her buy a copy for one rupee.
Plan: leave the scrap-paper box out on Friday.

qa.q: What did Simran name her newspaper?
qa.a: "The Colony Times."

qa.q: What does Simran's going quiet at about quarter to three suggest?
qa.a: It suggests her boredom had turned into an idea, and she was absorbed in making something of her own.

qa.q: What choice by Maria helped Simran's game appear, and why?
qa.a: Not rushing to fill the boredom with the tablet or a craft left space for Simran to invent the newspaper herself.

qa.q: How might the watchman feel about being interviewed by Simran?
qa.a: He might feel amused and quite pleased to be asked questions and to appear in her paper.

grounding: A child complains of boredom through a holiday afternoon, then, left unhurried, invents a newspaper game.

subtype: Restless boredom on a long afternoon [Actor]
passage:
Tuesday, at Nana's house

Diary, today was the BORINGEST day of the holidays. It rained all afternoon, the power went, and Nana was sleeping. No TV. No phone signal in the village. I said "I'm bored" to Nani so many times she started saying it back to me.
Kishore and I lay on the verandah looking at the rain for about a hundred years. Then I noticed the water running down the drain along the courtyard really fast. I tore a page from my old notebook and made a boat. Kishore made one too. We raced them from the tulsi pot to the gate. Then we made rules: a boat that sinks loses three points, a boat that gets stuck on a leaf can be poked once with a stick.
I won 14 to 11. Kishore says he wants a rematch tomorrow. I hope it rains.
Ujjwal

qa.q: Where did the boat race start and finish?
qa.a: From the tulsi pot to the gate.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal feel about the rain by the end of the day?
qa.a: The rain that made the day so boring became something Ujjwal hoped would come back, because it made the game possible.

qa.q: What would you tell Ujjwal's Nani about letting the children stay bored?
qa.a: That not hurrying to fill the afternoon gave them room to invent the boat race on their own.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel after losing 14 to 11?
qa.a: Kishore probably feels a bit competitive but excited, which is why he wants a rematch tomorrow.

grounding: A child complains of boredom on a rainy holiday afternoon until the empty time leads to an invented game.
